chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, who said:

Indeed, my mother had made a vow upon herself for Allah: if Allah were to return one of her children from something she feared for him, she would fast on the day he returns, as long as she lived. So she traveled with us to Mecca, and it became doubtful upon us; we did not know whether she should fast or break her fast. So I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about that, and informed him of what she had vowed upon herself. He said: 'She should not fast during the journey, for Allah has exempted her from His right regarding the fast, but she should fast what she has made upon herself [as the vow].'
He said: I asked, 'What do you think if she returns and neglects that?' He said: 'I fear that she might see in that which she vowed what she dislikes [i.e., a consequence or sign of displeasure].'

key_terms.أَبَا عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu Abdullah (Imam al-Sadiq, peace be upon him)
key_terms.حَقَّهُ: His right (referring to Allah's right of the fast)
key_terms.نَذْرًا: Vow (a voluntary commitment to perform an act of worship)

ai.seo_question: Does a traveler who made a vow to fast upon a specific event need to fast while traveling or only after returning?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the Shia juristic distinction between the obligatory fast of Ramadan and a specific vow (nadh), ruling that the traveler's exemption applies to the former but not the latter. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that while she is excused from fasting during the journey due to travel, she must still fulfill the vow upon her return, warning that neglecting it may lead to spiritual regret. This underscores the principle that personal vows retain their binding force even when general religious obligations are temporarily lifted.
